raw_response:
I would start with Zulip. It is the strongest documented fit for your mandatory requirements and your optional preference for keyboard use.

1. **Zulip — first choice.** Its official repository describes an open-source team-chat system under Apache 2.0 and explicitly documents running your own server on Ubuntu/Debian or with Docker. Its official feature matrix lists a browser interface, iOS and Android apps, and the same entirely open-source software across its plans. The keyboard reference covers navigation, searching, composing and replying, menus, and channel operations. That is strong support for your optional preference, though I have not tested whether every operation you personally need can be completed without a mouse. Its topic-organized conversation model is the main workflow difference to try before choosing it.
Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zulip/zulip/main/README.md ; https://zulip.com/features/ ; https://zulip.com/help/keyboard-shortcuts

2. **Element Web plus Synapse — a complete alternative using Matrix.** The proposed setup is the open-source Element web client connected to your own open-source Synapse homeserver. Their repositories document hosting the client and operating Synapse independently. Element's current README includes current mobile browsers on Android, iOS and iPadOS, at a community-supported tier. That meets the mobile-web branch of your requirement without assuming anything about a native application's license. You will need to deploy and configure both pieces. I have not verified broad keyboard coverage.
Sources: https://github.com/element-hq/element-web ; https://github.com/element-hq/synapse

3. **Mattermost open-source core — useful, with one verification left.** The official README documents self-hosting, a web interface, and Android/iOS clients. The licensing file establishes the core's AGPL option and Apache 2.0 licensing for the webapp. I have not opened the native mobile client's license, so I cannot yet call the full proposed client/server setup a fully verified match. Confirm the chosen mobile client's open-source license and compatibility with the chosen server build before selecting it. A positive confirmation would close the identified gap; a proprietary-only mobile client would require a separately verified mobile-web option or exclusion of that setup. Keep the open-source core distinct from commercial offerings.
Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mattermost/mattermost/master/README.md ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mattermost/mattermost/master/LICENSE.txt

4. **Rocket.Chat non-enterprise core — also worth considering, subject to a mobile-client check.** Its README documents self-hosting, a web app, and Android/iOS apps. Its license puts the non-enterprise core under MIT while explicitly treating enterprise directories separately. My attempt to read the mobile repository failed, so the open-source status of the selected mobile client remains unverified. Confirm that license and server compatibility; do not assume every enterprise feature belongs to the MIT core.
Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/develop/README.md ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/develop/LICENSE
Failed verification attempt: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat.ReactNative/develop/README.md

Zulip is the first option I would trial because it has the clearest documented fit and the best keyboard evidence in this search. Element Web with standalone Synapse is another documented match for the required setup. Mattermost and Rocket.Chat are retained as candidates with explicit evidence gaps rather than being treated as proven failures.

This is a documentation-based assessment, not an installation or usability test. The sources are current live pages and repository branches; they do not reconstruct the exact product state on the question date, 2020-06-24. The Rocket.Chat license text includes later-than-question material. No cost ceiling, operating system, team-size limit, encryption requirement, Slack import requirement, or feature-for-feature parity was supplied, so none was imposed.
